subject: Banking
title: How Check Clearing Works
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: How Check Clearing Works.

hook.text: When you deposit a check, your bank sends it to the writer's bank to collect the money. This is called clearing.

buildup.text: Before computers, banks exchanged physical checks daily at clearinghouses. Messengers carried bags full of paper.

discovery.text: In 1853, New York banks created a central clearinghouse. Instead of settling individually, they netted balances daily.

twist.text: Netting was brilliant. If Bank A owed Bank B $1M and Bank B owed Bank A $900K, only $100K actually moved.

climax.text: Clearinghouses reduced the money that needed to move by 90%. Efficiency through netting changed banking forever.

punchline.text: Instead of settling each check, banks net the difference. Elegant.

quiz.question: What does 'netting' in check clearing mean?
options: Banks offset mutual debts and only transfer the net difference

details.summary: Check clearing is the multi-day process where the payee's bank sends the check to the payer's bank through a clearinghouse, verifies funds are available, and transfers the money between the two accounts.
details.whyItMatters: The complexity of check clearing explains why deposited checks take days to fully clear and why check fraud persists. It is one of the oldest and least efficient payment settlement processes still in use.
takeaways: Electronic check images have replaced most physical check transport
Clearing typically takes 1 to 3 business days through the Federal Reserve
Banks may make funds available before the check fully clears

faq.question: Why do banks make funds available before a check clears?
faq.answer: Federal regulation requires banks to make portions of deposited checks available within set timeframes. This creates a float period where funds are available but the check has not been verified, which fraudsters exploit.

faq.question: What is the Check 21 Act?
faq.answer: The Check Clearing for the 21st Century Act of 2004 allowed banks to process electronic images of checks instead of physically transporting paper. This dramatically sped up clearing and reduced transportation costs.
